paragraphs.text: Abstract. A nitrogen-doped carbon nitride (g-C3N4-N) photocatalyst was synthesized by a one-step thermal polymerization of urea at 550 degrees C under air.
The crystal structure was characterized by X-ray diffraction, and the specific surface area measured by BET was 42.6 m2/g, roughly 1.8 times that of the undoped reference sample.

Under simulated sunlight (AM 1.5G, 100 mW/cm2), the g-C3N4-N sample degraded 92.5 percent of a 10 mg/L rhodamine B solution within 90 min, whereas the undoped sample reached only 61.3 percent under identical conditions.
Table 1. Comparison of photocatalysts: g-C3N4-N, degradation 92.5 percent, BET area 42.6 m2/g, band gap 2.41 eV; undoped g-C3N4, degradation 61.3 percent, BET area 23.7 m2/g, band gap 2.78 eV.

The authors attribute the enhanced activity to nitrogen doping, which narrows the band gap from 2.78 eV to 2.41 eV and improves charge separation; however, long-term cycling stability was not evaluated in this study.
Figure 1. Photocatalytic degradation curves of rhodamine B as a function of irradiation time for g-C3N4-N and the undoped reference.
Trapping experiments indicated that superoxide radicals were the dominant reactive species, while hydroxyl radical trapping showed no significant suppression of degradation.
Chen et al. (2024) reported a similar urea-derived carbon nitride with a BET area of 31.2 m2/g, lower than the value obtained here.
